headline: Google only saw question 1 of my 100-question quiz
summary: A developer discovered that Googlebot couldn't see 99% of their quiz content because it was hidden behind JavaScript interactions.
details: A developer built a quiz site where only one question is visible at a time, with buttons for 'Yes' and 'No'. This provides a better user experience, especially on mobile, and hides 99% of the content from search engines. However, this design choice led to a surprising SEO issue: Googlebot was only indexing the first question.

Upon investigation, the developer found that while Google runs JavaScript, it doesn't interact with the page like a user would. Since Googlebot doesn't click the 'Yes' or 'No' buttons, the rendered DOM still only shows the initial state: question 1. This is a common problem for interactive UIs like wizards, carousels, or components that load content lazily.

To fix this, the developer added a server component that renders all 100 questions as a plain, numbered list below the FAQ section. This list is generated from the same data array used by the quiz, ensuring consistency. The list is also beneficial for users who want to see upcoming questions or navigate directly to specific ones.

The developer implemented a simple test to verify the fix: fetch the page's HTML, strip scripts and styles, and then search for the content. After deploying the change, the live page was re-tested, confirming that all 100 questions were now present in the HTML. The developer then requested reindexing in Google Search Console.

headline_marked: AI video of victim [[quashed killer's sentence]] in Arizona court
headline: AI video of victim quashed killer's sentence in Arizona court
summary: An Arizona appeals court ruled that an AI-generated video message from a murder victim was improperly used in court, leading to a resentencing for the killer.
details: An Arizona road rage killer's sentence has been overturned because an AI-generated video of the victim was shown in court. Gabriel Paul Horcasitas was convicted of shooting Christopher Pelkey in 2021 and sentenced to 10 years.

Horcasitas' legal team appealed the sentence, arguing that the trial judge should not have allowed the AI video, created by Pelkey's family, to be presented before sentencing. The Arizona Court of Appeals agreed, stating the clip "crossed that line."

The court of appeals wrote that the AI video "presents a depiction of the victim and his thoughts created from the imaginings of the victim's sister," rather than documenting a real event. The victim's sister used voice recordings, videos, and pictures to recreate him.

In the AI video, the recreated Pelkey stated, "To Gabriel Horcasitas, the man who shot me, it is a shame we encountered each other that day in those circumstances. In another life, we probably could have been friends." He also expressed belief in forgiveness.

The judge who oversaw the original sentencing, Todd Lang, had appreciated the AI video at the time, saying he heard forgiveness and felt it was genuine. However, the appeals court's decision means Horcasitas will now be resentenced.
